newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian privatization minister Kokh quits.
newsitem.headline: Russian privatization minister Kokh quits.

text.p: Russian privatization chief Alfred Kokh has resigned and will be replaced by another ally of economic policy chief Anatoly Chubais.

A spokesman for President Boris Yeltsin said Wednesday that Kokh, who resigned as Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the State Property Committee, would be replaced in both posts by Maxim Boiko, currently deputy head of Yeltsin's administration.
Previously Boiko headed the Russian Privatization Center.
Both Kokh and Boiko are close to Chubais, who is one of two first deputy prime ministers and the main architect of market reforms in Yeltsin's government.
Kokh said he planned to set up his own company but did not disclose what kind of business it would be.
"He has long wanted to quit government service ... He is a high-class professional in the legal, financial and economic fields," his secretary Victoria Vergelskaya told Reuters.
She said his resignation was not linked to political controversy surrounding Russia's latest spate of state sell-offs.
Kokh has presided over a particularly stormy phase of Russian privatization and was singled out for criticism recently by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
The biggest sell-off, the sale last month of one quarter of telecoms company Svyazinvest, prompted an unprecedented outcry in media controlled by businessmen linked to the losing consortium.

The sale this month of a controlling 38 percent stake in Russia's biggest mining company, Norilsk Nickel, also proved controversial, with Chernomyrdin unsuccessfully trying to have the sale stopped at the last minute.

Kokh also halted the controversial privatization of Russia's biggest insurer, Rosgosstrakh, in June. Company management, which stood to win a large stake in the insurer, is suing the State Property Committee over the suspension.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, Kokh said he had tried to quit government service as early as 1995 but had been told that "first he must launch the process of cash privatization and make it work smoothly."
Recent sales, including Svyazinvest, which netted $1.88 billion for state coffers, showed the country was able to profit handsomely from privatization.
"Now I can go into the private sector with a quiet conscience," Kokh said.
